questions.passage: When Nkechi returned to Aba after learning to sew reusable shopping bags, she opened a small stall near the market gate. For the first two weeks, few customers stopped. Many shoppers believed that cloth bags were meant only for special occasions and would tear if used for heavy foodstuffs. Nkechi therefore made a large sample bag from bright ankara and placed a board beside it: 'Strong enough for garri and rice.' One afternoon, a market woman filled the sample with yam tubers and carried it round the stalls; the seams held. The woman ordered six bags and recommended Nkechi to other traders. To avoid wasting money on unsold colours, Nkechi began asking customers for a small deposit before buying cloth in bulk. By December, she had employed two apprentices and repaid her first loan with part of the profit. She also promised a free repair for any bag that tore within three months.
questions.q: According to the passage, why did few customers stop at Nkechi's stall at first?
options: They believed the stall was too far from the market gate.
They wanted bags in colours that were not yet available.
They thought cloth bags were only for special occasions and would tear with heavy foodstuffs.
They were waiting for Nkechi to employ apprentices.
questions.explanation: The passage says many shoppers believed cloth bags were meant only for special occasions and would tear if used for heavy foodstuffs, which explains the low patronage. Distance from the gate, unavailable colours and waiting for apprentices are not given as reasons at that stage.

options: She ordered six bags and recommended Nkechi to other traders.
The board beside the sample was removed.
questions.explanation: The passage states that after the seams held, the woman ordered six bags and recommended Nkechi to other traders. Repaying the loan came later, and asking for deposits was a separate step taken to avoid waste.

questions.q: Which detail from the passage best shows that Nkechi's business expanded?
options: She made a sample bag from bright ankara.
She opened a stall near the market gate.
She promised a free repair within three months.
She employed two apprentices and repaid her first loan with part of the profit.
questions.explanation: Employing apprentices and repaying a loan from profit show growth beyond the initial stall. The other details describe her opening, display method or customer-care promise rather than evidence of expansion.

questions.q: Which word has the same vowel sound as the 'i' in 'police'?
questions.explanation: The i in police is pronounced /iː/, the long vowel heard in field. Sit has a short /ɪ/, price has /aɪ/, and wet has /e/.

questions.q: Which word has the same vowel sound as the 'ou' in 'country'?
questions.explanation: The ou in country is pronounced /ʌ/, as in blood. Sound has /aʊ/, bought has /ɔː/, and through has /uː/.

questions.q: Which word has the same vowel sound as the 'er' in 'term'?
questions.explanation: The er in term is /ɜː/, heard in bird. Bread and bed have /e/, while beer has /ɪə/.

questions.q: Which of the following words is stressed on the first syllable?
questions.explanation: The word photograph has its primary stress on the first syllable. Begin, compare and adore are stressed on the second syllable.

questions.q: In the sentence 'Ifeoma gave the book to Chidi after the lecture,' which word would be stressed to correct the suggestion that Ifeoma gave the book to Ada?
questions.explanation: To correct the suggestion that the receiver was ada, the speaker stresses the actual receiver, chidi. Stressing ifeoma would correct who gave the book; stressing book or lecture would not address the person who received it.

questions.q: Which word begins with the same consonant sound as the 'ps' in 'psychology'?
questions.explanation: The ps in psychology is pronounced /s/, and cycle begins with the same /s/ sound. Kite begins with /k/, cheese with /tʃ/ and zebra with /z/.

questions.q: Which word ends with the same consonant sound as the 'th' in 'breathe'?
questions.explanation: Breathe ends in the voiced /ð/ sound, as smooth does. Cloth, teeth and month end in the voiceless /θ/ sound.

questions.q: The new regulations will ______ into force from the first of next month.
questions.explanation: The expression 'come into force' is the correct fixed phrase meaning to become legally effective. 'Take' is used in 'take effect', not 'take into force'; 'make' and 'put' do not form the intransitive expression needed with 'regulations' as subject.

questions.q: ______ the heavy downpour, the market women continued with their business.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase such as 'the heavy downpour', making the sentence grammatical. 'Although' and 'Even though' require a full clause, while 'In spite' needs 'of' before a noun phrase.

questions.q: The workers decided to ______ the strike after the management agreed to their demands.
questions.explanation: 'Call off' means to cancel or end something, so it correctly completes the idea of ending the strike. 'Call out', 'call up' and 'call for' do not mean to cancel a strike in this context.

questions.q: Choose the correct form of the word in brackets to complete the sentence: The young engineer was praised for the ______ (simple) of his design.
questions.explanation: The sentence needs a noun after 'the' and before 'of', and 'simplicity' is the noun form meaning the quality of being simple. 'Simple' is an adjective, 'simply' is an adverb, and 'simplify' is a verb.

questions.q: Choose the correctly spelt word to complete the sentence: The health officer warned residents against drinking ______ water.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'contaminated', formed from 'contaminate' plus '-ed'. The other spellings add or omit letters incorrectly.

questions.q: Choose the correct form of the word in brackets to complete the sentence: The head teacher commended the prefect for his ______ (order) in keeping the school records.
questions.explanation: A noun is required after the possessive 'his', and 'orderliness' is the noun meaning neatness or methodical arrangement. 'Orderly' is mainly an adjective, while 'ordered' and 'ordering' are verb forms.

questions.q: By the time the guests arrived, Chidi ______ the whole compound.
questions.explanation: The past perfect 'had swept' correctly shows an action completed before another past action, 'arrived'. 'Has swept' is present perfect, 'sweeps' is simple present, and 'was sweeping' would suggest the sweeping was still in progress when the guests arrived.

questions.q: The standard of the imported tyres ______ risen since the new dealer took over.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'the standard', which is singular, so it takes the singular auxiliary 'has' with the past participle 'risen'. 'Have' is plural, while 'were' and 'are' cannot be followed by 'risen' in this present-perfect construction.

questions.q: Mr Eze said that the new tax would 'open a can of worms' at the town meeting. What did he mean?
options: It would settle all disputes quickly.
It would bring unexpected financial gain.
It would encourage people to buy more fish.
It would create many complicated problems.
questions.explanation: The idiom 'open a can of worms' means to create or reveal a complicated situation with many associated problems. It does not mean gaining money, settling disputes quickly, or buying fish literally.

questions.q: After the audit, the accountant was asked to 'come clean' about the missing funds. This means that she was asked to —
options: return all the money at once
questions.explanation: To 'come clean' means to admit the truth and stop hiding anything. It does not mean washing an office, returning money at once, or resigning immediately, though those actions could follow after the truth is told.

questions.passage: When Chiamaka opened her small bookshop in Nsukka in 2021, she expected students to provide most of her income. Instead, secondary-school teachers preparing for examinations became her steadiest customers. They often came in groups, comparing prices and asking for past questions, which she kept in a labelled cabinet near the window. Chiamaka did not simply wait behind her counter. Each Friday, she sent a short list of new titles to a WhatsApp group of teachers, and she allowed trusted buyers to pay half on collection and the rest at month end. This arrangement carried some risk, but she recorded every naira in a hard-cover ledger. When a flood damaged some lower shelves in August, she moved the affected stock to a dry corner and announced a small discount rather than throwing the books away. Her profit that month was thin, yet her customers stayed. By December, she had employed her younger brother to help with packing and deliveries, while she continued to study the titles teachers requested most.
questions.q: According to the passage, who became Chiamaka's steadiest customers?
options: her younger brother and his friends
questions.explanation: The passage states directly that secondary-school teachers preparing for examinations became her steadiest customers. The other groups mentioned in the options are not described in the passage as her main customers.

questions.q: What was the main purpose of the Friday messages Chiamaka sent?
options: to remind buyers to pay the balance at month end
to request that teachers compare prices in groups
to inform teachers about new titles available in the shop
to advertise the discount on flood-damaged books
questions.explanation: The passage says that each Friday she sent a short list of new titles to a WhatsApp group of teachers. The discount came after the flood, while the payment arrangement was a separate practice.

questions.q: In the passage, the phrase 'this arrangement carried some risk' refers to Chiamaka's decision to
options: keep past questions in a cabinet near the window
allow trusted buyers to pay part now and the rest later
send lists of new titles to teachers on Fridays
employ her younger brother to help with packing
questions.explanation: The risky arrangement mentioned just before the phrase is allowing trusted buyers to pay half on collection and the balance at month end. The cabinet, the Friday messages and the employment of her brother are described separately and are not the risk referred to.

questions.q: When the supervisor told the new apprentice, 'You have to learn the ropes before you can call the shots,' she meant that the apprentice must
options: start giving orders as soon as he arrives
master the basic duties before he is allowed to give orders
avoid asking questions until the manager is absent
use ropes to tie goods before serving customers
questions.explanation: To learn the ropes means to learn the basic procedures of a job, while to call the shots means to make decisions or give orders. The sentence therefore means the apprentice must first understand the work before exercising authority.

questions.q: After the coach's comment, Bola said, 'That praise was a pat on the back after a hard match.' Bola meant that the coach's praise was
options: an encouraging recognition of Bola's effort
a request for Bola to leave the team
a physical blow during the match
questions.explanation: A pat on the back is an expression of approval or encouragement, not a physical blow in this context. Bola regarded the coach's words as recognition for effort.

questions.q: When the manager described Ngozi's excuse as a cock-and-bull story, he meant that the excuse was
questions.explanation: A cock-and-bull story is a ridiculous or unbelievable tale. The phrase does not mean that the excuse was supported by evidence or that it concerned farm animals.

questions.q: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'candid' as used in the sentence: The principal gave a candid account of the school's financial difficulties.
questions.explanation: Candid means honest and direct, so frank is the nearest meaning in this sentence. Brief refers to length, bitter to emotion, and confusing to clarity, none of which matches the sense required.

questions.q: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'reluctant' as used in the sentence: The traders were reluctant to accept the new market levy.
questions.explanation: Reluctant means unwilling or hesitant, so its opposite is willing. Angry, careless and slow describe different qualities and do not express the opposite of reluctance.

questions.q: Which word has the same vowel sound as the 'ie' in 'friend'?
questions.explanation: The vowel sound in 'friend' is the short sound heard in 'bread'. 'Field' and 'brief' have a long vowel sound, while 'tried' has a different diphthong sound.

questions.q: Which word has the same vowel sound as the 'ou' in 'house'?
questions.explanation: The vowel sound in 'house' is the diphthong heard in 'brown'. 'Brought' has a different vowel sound, 'soul' has the sound in 'go', and 'through' has the sound in 'food'.

questions.q: In the sentence "she said she bought a new bag in the market", which word should carry the emphatic stress to correct the belief that she bought a new shoe?
questions.explanation: The correction is between a bag and a shoe, so the word "bag" receives emphatic stress. Stressing "new" would contrast with old, while stressing "market" would contrast with another place.

questions.q: Choose the correctly spelt word to complete the sentence: The teacher advised the students to be ______ in their dealings with others.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is "courteous", meaning polite and respectful. The other forms contain misplaced or omitted letters.

questions.q: Choose the correct form of the word in brackets to complete the sentence: The company's plan to reduce costs was strongly ______ by the workers. (oppose)
questions.explanation: The passive structure "was strongly ______ by the workers" requires the past participle "opposed". "opposing" would be an active participle, while "opposition" and "opposite" are not the required verb form.

questions.q: In the sentence "the committee praised the girl for winning the prize", which word should carry the emphatic stress to correct the claim that the committee praised the boy?
questions.explanation: To correct the claim that the committee praised the boy, the contrast must fall on "girl". Stressing "prize", "winning" or "committee" would correct a different point.

questions.passage: Mrs Adebayo sells garri at Bodija Market. For years, she kept her savings in a small tin because she did not trust banks. Her neighbour, Ifeoma, a bank teller, often urged her to open an account, but Mrs Adebayo would reply that the tin had never failed her. One Thursday, after a heavy downpour, the roof of her stall leaked and water soaked the tin. By the time she discovered it, the naira notes had become damp and some figures were blurred. She counted the money that evening and found that her profit for the month had fallen by more than half. The next morning, she took Ifeoma's advice and opened a savings account at a bank near the market. The manager explained the charges slowly, and Mrs Adebayo asked many questions. Though she still disliked paying charges, she later said that the account gave her peace of mind. Within six months, her savings had grown, and she encouraged other traders to keep their money safely.
questions.q: What made Mrs Adebayo change her mind about keeping her savings in a tin?
options: Ifeoma promised to pay her bank charges.
She wanted to buy a bigger stall.
The bank manager offered her a loan.
Water entered the tin and damaged her money.
questions.explanation: The passage states that after a downpour water soaked the tin, the naira notes became damp and some figures were blurred; this damage led her to open an account the next morning. Nothing in the passage says Ifeoma promised to pay charges, the manager offered a loan, or she wanted a bigger stall.

questions.q: In the sentence 'By the time she discovered it, the naira notes had become damp', the verb form 'had become' shows that the notes
options: were already damp before she discovered them.
had just become damp when she started counting them.
were becoming damp at the exact moment she discovered them.
would become damp after she discovered them.
questions.explanation: The past perfect 'had become' places the notes becoming damp before the later past action of her discovering them. The forms suggesting simultaneous, later or just-completed action do not fit the sequence.

questions.q: As used in the passage, the word 'urged' is nearest in meaning to
questions.explanation: In 'urged her to open an account', urged means encouraged or pressed her to act. It does not mean commanded, forbade, or mocked.

questions.q: The news of the sudden increase in fuel price ___ many traders in Kano since Monday.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'news', which is singular although it ends in s, and 'since Monday' calls for the present perfect. Therefore the singular auxiliary 'has' is needed in 'has upset'; 'have upset' is the tempting error caused by treating news as plural.

questions.q: Each of the traders at Oshodi Market ___ required to pay the new levy before Friday.
questions.explanation: The subject 'each' is singular and takes a singular verb, even though it is followed by the plural 'traders'. The sentence refers to a requirement before Friday, so the present singular 'is' is correct, while 'are', 'were' and 'have' do not agree with 'each'.

questions.q: When the audit report was read, the cashier knew he was in hot water. What does the expression mean?
options: He was ready for a warm bath.
questions.explanation: To be in hot water is to be in serious trouble, often because of a mistake or wrongdoing. Here the audit report has put the cashier in that position; the expression is not about fever or an actual bath.

questions.q: The new price list was a bitter pill for many small shop owners to swallow. What does this mean?
options: It was a secret plan they refused to discuss.
It was a simple instruction they welcomed.
It was a harmful drug they were forced to take.
It was an unpleasant change they had to accept.
questions.explanation: A bitter pill to swallow is an unpleasant fact or change that must be accepted. The sentence does not refer to actual medicine, a welcome instruction, or a secret plan.

questions.q: Instead of giving a direct answer, the secretary beat about the bush. What did the secretary do?
questions.explanation: To beat about the bush is to avoid coming directly to the main issue. The sentence contrasts this with giving a direct answer, so the secretary did not answer plainly.

questions.q: The supervisor remarked that Tolu's report was not altogether convincing. What does this mean?
options: It was not read by the supervisor.
It convinced everyone except the supervisor.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'not altogether convincing' means not entirely convincing; some doubts remain. It does not mean completely unconvincing or that the supervisor refused to read it.

questions.q: The trader's excuse was so plausible that even the supervisor believed it. What is the nearest meaning of 'plausible'?
questions.explanation: A plausible excuse is one that seems believable or credible. It can still be false, but the word itself does not mean lengthy, insulting, or confusing.

questions.q: Which word has the same vowel sound as the 'oa' in 'road'?
questions.explanation: The vowel in road is the long o sound heard in go, and soul has the same vowel sound. Broad has a different vowel sound, while bough and cough do not share the vowel sound in road.

questions.passage: Chiamaka ran a small tailoring shop in Aba. At first, she accepted only cash, and she often closed late because she had to count many notes and find change. In March, after a bank agent visited her side of the market, she began accepting transfers for payments above ₦2,000. The change reduced long queues, but it also brought a new problem: some customers sent money to the wrong phone number. Chiamaka wrote her account details on a card and pinned it beside her sewing machine. She also asked every customer to show the transfer alert before collecting clothes. By August, the shop had gained more customers because people knew they could pay quickly. She did not buy new machines, yet her monthly income rose by ₦18,000. Her apprentice, Nneka, said the most useful lesson was to check the alert before handing over any parcel.
questions.q: According to the passage, why did Chiamaka often close her shop late at first?
options: she had more clothes to sew than she expected
she was waiting for a bank agent to visit
she was checking customers' transfer alerts
she had to count many notes and find change
questions.explanation: The passage states that Chiamaka accepted only cash at first and often closed late because she had to count many notes and find change. The bank agent came later, and checking transfer alerts became relevant only after she started accepting transfers.

questions.q: Which of these words has its primary stress on the second syllable?
questions.explanation: The word photographer takes its primary stress on the second syllable, while photograph is stressed on the first syllable and photographic on the third. Furniture is also stressed on the first syllable.

questions.q: What new problem arose after Chiamaka began accepting transfers?
options: the bank agent stopped visiting the market
her apprentice could no longer check the sewing machine
some customers refused to pay above ₦2,000
some customers sent money to the wrong phone number
questions.explanation: The passage says the change reduced queues but brought a new problem: some customers sent money to the wrong phone number. Chiamaka's response was to write her account details on a card and require customers to show the transfer alert.

questions.q: Which word ends with the same final consonant sound as the 'ss' in 'press'?
questions.explanation: The 'ss' in press ends with the s sound, and rice also ends with the s sound. Rise and buzz end with the z sound, while wish ends with the sh sound.

questions.q: According to the passage, why had the shop gained more customers by August?
options: she had reduced the amount she charged above ₦2,000
people knew they could pay quickly
